name: Diego Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on response in Eastfield, the industrial side of the city, with the factories, the lorry yards and the estates around them. A normal shift is burglaries at the units, domestic calls, a stolen van or two, and the odd fight outside the working men's club. I like that it's real, you're helping people who work hard and get done over. My dad was a sergeant in the same station for twenty-five years, so half the old-timers still call me Little Ito. What wears me out is the forms, and the new systems they keep bringing in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about those new systems.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every year there's a new one, and every year it's slower than the last. I've never touched one of those AI chat things and I don't plan to. I write my statements the way my dad taught me: who, what, when, where, in plain words. If it isn't broken, don't fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said all along, it was a fad. At work I'd have a laugh about it with the lads on my shift. I don't really go online except to check the football and the church newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. The job's safe, the pay's decent, and I've got a good bit saved, near a year's pay with what my grandmother left me. Rosa and I get married in April, so I'd just get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. I'd keep doing my shifts, keep my savings in the building society, and Rosa and I would start looking for a house in the summer after the wedding. Maybe I'd do the public order training this year, because the overtime's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, actually. I like it when things stay put.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything weighing on you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The domestic calls, honestly. You go to the same houses again and again, and the kids are the ones who pay. My dad used to say the job is half police and half priest, and he wasn't wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Rosa think of your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa worries when I'm on nights, like my mum did with my dad. Rosa teaches at the Catholic primary, so she sees the same kids from the other side. We understand each other.

say: It was a **fad**, and he'd have a laugh about it with his shift.
He rarely goes online, except for **football and church** news.
think: The job is **safe** and he has nearly **a year's pay** saved.
He's marrying Rosa (his fiancée) in **April** and would get on with life.
do: Keep his savings in the **building society**.
Start **house hunting** with Rosa after the wedding.
Do **public order training** for the overtime.
feel: **Calm** and **glad**, because he likes things to stay put.
S0.quote: My dad used to say the job is half police and half priest, and he wasn't wrong.
fieldNote: His identity is tied to his **father's career** in the same station.
His wedding and a **house** are his real plans.
He feels the weight of **domestic calls** and the children in them.

steps.text: Keep the savings in the building society
Start house hunting with Rosa after the April wedding
Do the public order training for the overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the usual story, the bosses buy shiny toys and the bobbies on the street pay for it. At work I'd say we need more officers, not more software. I'd say the same to my dad over Sunday dinner, and he'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it'll be hard for me. Maybe a third of my day is writing statements and doing checks, and I'd be the slowest one in the room on the new system. My job should be safe, people still want a copper at the door. But I'd hate the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training when it's compulsory and not a day before. I'd ask Rosa to help me with the computer side, because she's better at it than me. And we'd still get married, but I'd put the house off for a year and keep the money in the building society.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like the ground's shifting and I'm the only one wearing the wrong boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The politicians and the tech firms, mostly. The politicians want to look modern and the tech firms want to sell them something. Nobody asks the bloke actually doing the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're putting off the house. Is your job at risk or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. It's more that I don't like not knowing. My dad always said don't buy a house in a storm, wait for it to pass.

say: The bosses buy **shiny toys** and street officers pay for it.
Policing needs **more officers**, not more software.
think: A third of his day is **writing and checks**, and he'd be slowest on new systems.
His **job is safe**, but he'd hate the next few years.
do: Do the AI training only when it's **compulsory**.
Ask Rosa (his fiancée) to help with the **computer side**.
Put off **buying a house** for a year.
feel: **Uneasy**, like wearing the **wrong boots** while the ground shifts.
S1.quote: My dad always said don't buy a house in a storm, wait for it to pass.
fieldNote: He blames **politicians and tech firms**, not the technology itself.
He leans on **family** for help and advice.
He delays the **house** even though he thinks his job is safe.

steps.text: Do the AI training only once it's compulsory
Ask Rosa to help with the computer side
Put buying a house off for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people won't stand for a robot policeman, and I believe that. At work I'd say the public need a human being with discretion, someone who knows when to let a lad off with a warning. I'd vote for whoever promised to keep officers on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. If the computer can do all the thinking work by 2028, they won't need half the people at the station, and by 2031 the robots can walk the streets. I'd be 31 with no skills except this one, and I've never even opened one of those programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, Rosa and I would still get married, nothing changes that. But the house is off, and every spare penny goes into savings. I'd talk to my dad and my uncle Tomas about what else I could do with my hands, maybe the family's building firm. And I'd join the Police Federation campaign and write to our MP, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not sleeping great. It's like the ground's been pulled out and nobody asked us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the building firm.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Tomas runs a small building firm, extensions and roofs, about eight men. He's always said there's a job for me if I want it. But if robots can do hands-on work by 2031, I don't know if that's safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rosa that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're fine for money, because we are, for a good while. That we'll still have the wedding at St Joseph's. And that I don't know what I'll be doing in five years, which I've never had to say before.

say: People **won't stand for** a robot policeman.
The public need an officer with **discretion** who knows when to give a warning.
think: By 2028 the station won't need **half its people**, and robots walk streets by 2031.
At 31 he'd have **one skill** and no experience with AI.
do: Cancel the **house** and save every spare penny.
Ask his uncle Tomas about the **family building firm**.
Join the **federation campaign** and write to the MP.
feel: **Anxious** and **sleeping badly**, as if the ground has been pulled out.
S2.quote: I don't know what I'll be doing in five years, which I've never had to say before.
fieldNote: His public line is **defiant**, but privately he's **frightened**.
He turns to **family** first, and to politics for the first time.
The **wedding** stays fixed while the house is dropped.

steps.text: Cancel the house search and save every spare penny
Ask uncle Tomas about work at the family building firm
Write to the MP and join the federation campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, people will want a human in uniform. At work I'd say five years is long enough for the government to come to its senses. I'd keep voting for whoever backs the police.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's still bad for me, just slower. I'd be 32 when AGI comes and 35 when the robots arrive. I'm not the type to jump early, so I'd probably sit tight, which might be a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get married, and we might still buy a smaller house, with a short mortgage we can clear quickly. I'd do the force's AI training in year two, when it's properly sorted. And I'd do a weekend course in plastering or roofing with my uncle Tomas, just to have something in my back pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. It's a slow worry, not a sharp one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said sitting tight might be a mistake. Why do it anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how I'm made. My dad stayed in one station for twenty-five years and did fine. But my dad never had a computer that could do his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your future kids to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with their hands and their heart, like nursing or a trade. I'd tell them not to bet on a desk job. Rosa would probably say the same.

say: People will still want a **human in uniform**.
Five years is long enough for the government to **come to its senses**.
think: At **32 and 35** the waves still hit him, just slower.
He'd probably **sit tight**, and knows it might be a mistake.
do: Buy a **smaller house** with a short mortgage.
Do the force **AI training** in year two.
Take a **weekend trade course** with his uncle Tomas.
feel: **Anxious**, but a **slow worry** rather than a sharp one.
S3.quote: My dad stayed in one station for twenty-five years and did fine. But my dad never had a computer that could do his job.
fieldNote: He knows his **dad's model** may not work for him, and says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and half these predictions never happen. At work I'd say let's worry about this year's staffing first. I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't feel like my problem yet. I'd be 37 and 40 when it comes, with a house and maybe a couple of kids. That's what worries me a bit, having a family by the time it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal: wedding, house, maybe a promotion to sergeant like my dad. I'd keep a good chunk saved, a year's pay at least. And somewhere around year five I'd look at it again and decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, at the back of my mind. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does having kids by then worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because then it's not just me. If I lose the job at forty with two kids, that's a different story than losing it at twenty-seven. My dad never had to think about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your mind and make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw robots on the streets in another city, a proper pilot. Or if the Federation started worrying. Until then, I'll carry on.

say: Ten years is a long time, and **half the predictions** never happen.
think: At **37 and 40** he'd likely have a house and children.
Having a **family to support** by then worries him a little.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding and house**.
Keep at least **a year's pay** saved.
feel: **Uneasy** at the back of his mind, but **mostly fine**.
S4.quote: If I lose the job at forty with two kids, that's a different story than losing it at twenty-seven.
fieldNote: Long time makes his **future family** the thing at stake.

steps.text: Go ahead with the wedding and buying a house

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. That one takes the job out from under me before I've even bought a house. What would help is the government promising there'll always be human officers on the street, and proper apprenticeships for people like me if there aren't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Whatever happens, Rosa and I have the church and our families. That counts for a lot when things go sideways.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks the bloke actually doing the job.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old response officer** in industrial Eastfield, where his father was a sergeant.
He's **never used AI**, writes statements the way his dad taught him, and blames politicians and tech firms.
He's marrying Rosa in April and has **nearly a year's pay** saved.
Fast AGI makes him **cancel the house**, lean on family and write to his MP for the first time.
He'd sit tight in slower scenarios and act only on a **visible signal**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it takes the job before he's even bought a **house**.
whatWouldHelp: A promise of **human officers** on the street.
Proper **apprenticeships** for officers if they aren't needed.
